articles.title: Iran warns against any new escalation in the war, asks Trump to heed the popular will after midterm drubbing
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: No amount of rhetoric and threats of aggression will undermine its people’s will to protect its sovereignty and national integrity, Iran reiterated in the context of talks about the Donald Trump administration’s possible escalation in the war after being crushed in the US midterm elections. Though Trump admitted that the US-Israeli war on Iran was the main factor in his Republican Party’s losses in the November 3 midterm elections, he attempted to justify his decision to go to the war and even said he will do it again if necessary. In yet another TV interview after the results were announced on Wednesday, Trump even hinted that the US may have to do “something big” in order to make sure that Iran never gets nuclear weapons. Iran has always maintained it never wanted to develop nuclear weapons and its nuclear program is legal and for peaceful purposes only and called the US-Israeli war, launched in February, illegal. Reacting to US election results, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, speaker of the Iranian parliament and head of its negotiating team, asked the Trump administration to heed to the will of the American people and stop the war. “Conscience or cost of living, Americans said no to war, and we endorse this message. If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our no come with a nightmare,” Qalibaf said in a post on X. US is the greatest threat to NPT Calling the US “the greatest threat” to the nuclear non-proliferation regime, the official spokesperson of Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs Esmail Baghaei had warned on Monday against any normalization of nuclear military threats. Baghaei’s reaction came hours after journalist Tucker Carlson, citing unknown sources, had claimed that the US is under Israeli pressure to use nuclear weapons against Iran any day after the midterm elections. Iran claimed that such “explicit or implicit threats against a country’s nuclear facilities and alluding to the use of specific weapons effectively encourages actors to violate fundamental international treaties.” Earlier in October, various US officials had also threatened the use of “the mother of all bombs” on Iran. Reacting to fresh threats of escalation in the war, going on for eight months now, various Iranian officials have warned of strong and unprecedented retaliation. Esmail Qaani, head of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Forces said on Wednesday that any new attack will lead to a multi-front war in the region and may even threaten navigation through the Bab al-Mandab in the Red Sea. Repeating the Iranian claims that Trump “gambled on war with Iran after being misled by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu,” Qaani pointed out that the joint force of the Resistance in the region should not be undermined. He claimed that all the resistance fronts in the region, in Yemen, Lebanon, and Iraq, are united like never before and have pleaded loyalty to the Supreme Leader. “Those irresponsible US leaders should know that today the entire Resistance is one front with unity across different arenas. Therefore do not calculate the depth of the front based on weapons range alone; you must also factor in the depth of the Resistance,” Ghani told Sepah News. Not even the slightest submissive inclination In a message to the nation on the occasion of the National Day for Fighting Global Arrogance (Aban 13) on Wednesday Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned against “even the slightest submissive inclination towards domineering enemy” and asked the government to make “Iran ever stronger.” Aban 13 is celebrated in Iran on November 4 every year to mark the occasion of Iranian students occupying the US embassy in Tehran after the Islamic Revolution in 1979. The occupation, which lasted for over a year, was launched after it was claimed that the embassy was supporting pro-Shah elements and trying to sabotage the revolution. Any concession to the Americans “will squander the great capital acquired through the blood of martyrs and the sacrifices of all sections of the nation, and will embolden the arrogant enemy to make further excessive demands and commit further acts of aggression and war,” Khamenei said. He underlined that the successive US administrations have consistently worked to undermine Iran and its Islamic Revolution since 1979 and repeatedly faced defeats. Referring to the ongoing war against Iran as “the self-inflicted disgrace of the arrogant powers,” Khamenei claimed that it has led to the “declining power and domination, in both its military hard power dimension and its international soft-power dimension” and caused the US “an irreversible fall” and “accelerated the process of its collapse.” More tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz At least six oil tankers were damaged after they hit sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday and early morning Thursday, the IRGC claimed . It claimed that all the ships were trying to violate the Iranian restrictions and attempting to cross the Strait using the “unauthorized” route in the Omani waters. Four ships were hit on Wednesday while two more ships were hit in the early morning of Thursday. The IRGC also claimed two tug boats were also damaged because of the explosion of the sea mines. A day after the reports claimed the US carried out fresh attacks on its Qesham Island, Iran claimed on Wednesday it drowned yet another US MQ-1 drone. This was the 15th such drone destroyed by Iran since the beginning of the war in February.

articles.title: Follow the money: billionaire spending on the 2026 midterms
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: OpenSecrets published its list of top donors to outside groups this election cycle, and the top ten is a “who’s who” of billionaires: Elon Musk, casino magnate Miriam Adelson, former New York City mayor Michael Bloomberg, and tech oligarchs Benjamin Horowitz, Marc Andreessen, and Paul Singer all made the list. And although Republicans outraised and outspent Democrats across the board, the real story isn’t the party split. It’s who is writing the checks, and what they’re buying. In particular, three special interest groups spent historic amounts to capture Congress: AIPAC, Big Tech, and crypto. Below are some of the most egregious examples, but this is far from an exhaustive list. AIPAC AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to federal candidates and political committees this election cycle, through September 30. What happened after September 30? Here’s where it gets interesting. Since the genocide in Gaza began three years ago, more and more candidates are getting heat for taking AIPAC money, and support for Israel has become a massive political liability So in October, AIPAC publicly announced it would no longer be issuing endorsements or making direct contributions to candidates and PACs. But don’t be fooled: AIPAC isn’t stopping its spending, it’s only changing the way it spends. Instead of directly funding pro-Israel candidates themselves, the organization will now encourage individual donors to contribute to candidates and continue channeling funds through its affiliated super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP). In 2024, the UDP, functionally a cover for AIPAC money, spent over $9.8 million to unseat progressives New York representative Jamaal Bowman and another $5.2 million against Missouri representative Cori Bush. Both lost their races. In 2026, Bush ran and lost again after the UDP injected another $2 million into the race in favor of her opponent Wesley Bell. But AIPAC is now so toxic that its biggest investment in the primaries, the Michigan Democratic race between Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed, turned out to be a complete failure. AIPAC and its affiliated groups dumped $30 million into the race, trying to ensure staunch Israel supporter Haley Stevens would win the primary – but this made her a regular target of attack by her opponent Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens lost. After Stevens’s defeat, the UDP desperately poured $9 million into supporting El-Sayed’s Republican opponent Mike Rogers in the general election as a last-minute hail mary. They again failed. Another important race that AIPAC was betting on in the midterms was the one between progressive Democrat Aisha Wahab and her more moderate, police-union backed challenger Melissa Hernandez, also a Democrat, in California’s 14th Congressional District. Wahab ran on a platform of affordable housing and healthcare, worker protections, public education, and expanded access to food assistance. She has also explicitly called what’s going on in Gaza as a “genocide,” something that Hernandez declined to do. Wahab won the special election in August to finish Eric Swalwell’s term after he resigned over sexual assault allegations. She then faced Hernandez again in November’s election. UDP spent $1.2 million to block Wahab, including $800,000 on attack ads alone. Because they knew they could not attack Wahab over lack of support for Israel, they went after her public safety voting record. And that goes to show what a massive liability support for Israel has become. And let’s not forget the individual billionaire donors and how they shape Israeli policy. Just to name a few: Robert Kraft, the sports mogul billionaire who kicked Macklemore off of Ed Sheeran’s tour a couple of months ago, unsurprisingly is a major donor to the United Democracy Project and AIPAC, having donated several million dollars to both in the last decade. Miriam Adelson – Las Vegas casino magnate, pro-Israel megadonor – dropped over $66 million this cycle toward Republican groups and PACs, making her of the top individual donors of the entire midterm. And then there’s Hedge fund billionaire Paul Singer . This midterm cycle, he gave $49 million to Republican-aligned PACs and $2.6 million to the UDP. BIG TECH Big Tech billionaires showed up in a big way this year. Elon Musk took the number one spot for highest donor: $446 million to Republican candidates and PACs. Over $200 million of that went toward Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. But it’s not just Paxton. Musk also donated $5 million to Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor. Texas is one state where Elon was massively invested since he moved both Tesla’s and Space X’s corporate headquarters there from California. And in those years he’s cozied up to Texas state leaders to benefit from lucrative state contacts and tax breaks, so the millions of dollars he’s dropping in these midterms is just a small drop in the bucket for him to make sure that continues. Paxton and Abbott both lost their races. But Musk was far from the only tech oligarch invested in these midterms. Benjamin Horowitz, half of the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, spent over $55 million. His firm partner Marc Andreessen gave over $43 million . OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife Anna Brockman contributed $50 million . These four are particularly significant because they launched Leading the Future, a PAC whose mission includes funding candidates committed to blocking AI regulation and cutting China out of the AI race. In fact, the Brockmans’ $50 million was evenly split between Leading the Future and MAGA, Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC. CRYPTO And finally, crypto. Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, co-founders of Gemini crypto exchange, contributed nearly a combined $24 million this cycle. Most of their individual donations also went to MAGA Inc. to support Trump. Ripple Labs Chris Larsen gave at least $22.5 million of his own money to candidates and super PACs for the midterm elections. At least $12 million of that went toward opposing California’s proposed 5% billionaire wealth tax. Larsen also donated millions to the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC, which is spending millions to unseat incumbent Republicans who voted to end renewable energy incentives under Biden. However, Larsen has also said Invest in Tomorrow is getting ready to go after DSA soon. In an interview with Bloomberg , he warned: “We’re going to take out some of these DSA people that are standing in the way. There’s no time to waste.” Fairshake, crypto’s own political action committee, and its affiliated PACs dropped $95 million in this cycle. Fairshake backed 33 House incumbents this midterms, publicly disclosing at least $1 million in donations into the campaigns of candidates. Some of them hold key House committee positions which could shape future legislation on crypto: Republicans Bryan Steil of Wisconsin, who chairs a digital assets subcommittee and French Hill of Arkansas and Bill Huizenga of Michigan, the chair and vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, respectively. Fairshake also contributed $1 million to Democrats Janelle Bynum of Oregon, Derek Tran of California, and Steven Horsford of Nevada. House Ways and Means Committee chair Jason Smith, who has spent the last year trying to subpoena us at BT over our funding, is also backed by Fairshake, but they haven’t publicly disclosed how much they’ve contributed to his campaign. Smith, as chair, has introduced crypto legislation and tax reforms to, in his own words, “ensure the United States is the crypto capital of the world.” Whether it’s foreign policy, AI deregulation, or crypto protectionism, $12 billion bought a whole lot of access this election. What better encapsulates the rule of billionaires in the US better than this midterm cycle, where your choices to vote were for AIPAC, Big Tech, or crypto.

articles.title: Ireland to explore scenarios for constitutional future, including unity
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin recently announced plans to establish a government body to prepare for different scenarios for the country’s constitutional future, including the possibility of a united Ireland. A first round of updates about this plan are expected before the end of the year. In addition to outlining the scenario of a unitary Irish state, the body would also be tasked to prepare for a possible continuation of the existing situation, and “a future united Ireland in which Northern Ireland would remain a devolved entity, maintaining its own separate assembly and government, civil services, public services and police,” Martin said in an interview with The Irish Times in late October. “Sinn Féin believes that a united Ireland is the best future for all our people,” party leader Mary Lou McDonald stated in response. “Ending partition and bringing our country together offers the biggest opportunity to build a stronger economy, deliver better public services and create a fairer, reconciled society across the whole island.” Sinn Féin: unification would strengthen Ireland economically and politically Martin’s announcement came four months after parliamentarians voted on a Sinn Féin bill on reunification, which proposed deadlines for the government to develop a plan for the organization of public services and other areas of life in a united Ireland. Sinn Féin has argued for years that reunification would bring an opportunity to strengthen the island politically and economically, providing space for planning jobs and creating a unified healthcare system. “Through Unity, we can build the best education and childcare systems for every child and young person,” McDonald said earlier this year. “We can strengthen public services, tackle poverty, and build a fair society in which disabled people and those who care are supported to live lives of equal citizens.” The proposal, named the Planning for Constitutional Change Bill, also proposed a citizens’ assembly to ensure different perspectives are represented. Read more: A new spring for Irish unity In July, Martin’s Fianna Fáil and government partner Fine Gael voted against the Sinn Féin proposal, citing concerns over the bill’s time limitations and participation models. At the time, McDonald defended the timeliness of initiating reunification from the Irish side as the Good Friday Agreement approaches its 30th anniversary. “There has been nothing rushed, hasty or pre-emptive about this process,” McDonald said . “Over the last three decades, we had big challenges, disagreements, political confrontations, we have had high and lows – of that there is no doubt.” “However, the peace is secure. It is robust, resilient and commands wide support. It is now time to write the next chapter. The chapter of reunification.” A counter-reaction against unity momentum? Part of the responsibility for building this process, however, also rests with the British government – which is tasked with organizing a referendum if it becomes apparent that a majority of people in the north of Ireland would support leaving the United Kingdom. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham oscillated on this issue in recent appearances. In August, he described a border poll as “off the table.” His reaction was followed by an initiative launched by pro-independence parties from Wales, Scotland and Ireland, who signed a memorandum of understanding in September, pledging joint efforts toward self-determination. Watch: Is the UK breaking up? Ireland, Scotland & Wales unite for independence Some critics have also emphasized attempts to derail growing talks about reunification, including in the context of recent events on Garvaghy Road . In late September, members of the Portadown community organized protests and resistance to attempts by the Orange Order’s Drumcree march to pass through the largely Catholic area. Thousands gathered at Garvaghy Road. Photo: Sinn Fein “What happened at Garvaghy Road is a manufactured political crisis, which has been over two years in the making,” wrote Sinn Fein’s Declan Kearney . “The subtext to what is happening is the next year’s Assembly and council elections, and the objective of removing Sinn Fein as the largest party in the north and Michelle O’Neill from the position of First Minister.” “The current perfect storm of whipped up sectarian polarization and political instability is a pre-meditated counter-reaction to the growing momentum for Irish unity,” he added. “This is being driven by those sections of the British state, which are determined to prevent the right to national self-determination, and holding a unity referendum.”

articles.title: The bees in the city: organizing China’s delivery workers in Ganzhou
articles.author: Tings Chak
articles.content: At the entrance to Xingfuli, a residential compound in Ganzhou, Jiangxi province, a bulletin board displays the names, photographs, and phone numbers of the people responsible for managing the neighborhood. Though an ordinary bulletin board at first appearance, among the building representatives and Communist Party members is an unexpected name: Kang Jiafei, a food delivery worker who is also listed as a community “grid worker.” China has more than ten million food delivery workers, part of a rapidly growing global workforce whose lives are organized by algorithms, tight deadlines, and orders that take them across the city. They are among the most visible workers on China’s streets, yet often have no fixed workplace, no place to rest between orders, and limited access to conventional forms of employment protection. Their working hours are fragmented, their movements dictated by the next delivery. What, then, does it mean for one of these workers to have a recognized role in governing a residential community? In China, urban neighborhoods are divided into small geographical units known as grids (网格), with designated workers who monitor local conditions, respond to residents’ concerns, and coordinate with public departments. Kang is one of fifty delivery workers in Ganzhou’s Zhanggong District who have taken on this additional role. During my visit in October, Wuzhifeng Road Community Party secretary Yin Guozhu, responsible for this community, explained how it works. Delivery workers like Kang know the neighborhood through their daily deliveries. When he notices a blocked fire exit, debris near a lift, or another hazard, he reports it to the property management staff. Between orders, he also distributes the community’s anti-fraud leaflets. During recent typhoon weeks, riders who encountered fallen branches blocking drains cleared what they could and reported larger obstructions to the community, which contacted the responsible departments. “Our information is collected up layer by layer,” Yin explained. She calls the riders “mobile probes”: in places community workers cannot see or reach in time, they provide first-hand information. The same mobility that makes these workers difficult to organize also gives them intimate knowledge of the city’s streets and neighborhoods – knowledge that can now serve the wider community. In 2020, the widely read investigation Trapped in the System 《困在系统里》documented the tightening grip of delivery algorithms on these workers in China: a three-kilometer delivery window that fell from an hour in 2016 to only thirty-eight minutes by 2018. Riders described themselves as “racing with death, wrestling with the traffic police, befriending red lights.” The sociologist Sun Ping , after seven years of fieldwork, described the condition as “transitional labor” – work suspended between employment and informality, in which the transition becomes permanent and the delivery economy runs like a great “furnace”, constantly burning as workers rotate through it. Since 2021, national measures have sought to clarify platform companies’ responsibilities and extend labor protections in these “new forms of employment,” notably in the gig economy. An occupational injury insurance program , piloted from 2022 and expanded nationwide in 2026, places its premium obligations on platforms. Days before my visit, a draft regulation on protecting workers in new employment forms opened for public comment. Alongside these regulatory efforts, the Party has been extending its organizational work among workers dispersed across the platform economy. A workforce without a fixed workplace lacks many of the spaces where workers’ welfare and social life have traditionally been anchored. One of the most immediate problems has a simpler name: the riders’ “four difficulties” – eating, drinking water, resting, and finding a toilet, so the infrastructure has moved to the street. The All-China Federation of Trade Unions has helped establish more than 186,000 outdoor worker rest stations nationwide, aiming to ensure that outdoor workers can find a place to rest, drink water, or charge their phones within a fifteen-minute journey. In Zhanggong District, thirty-three Qianxin stations can be found through phone map apps. They take their name from Qian (虔), an old name for Ganzhou, and xin (新), referring to the new employment groups. President Xi Jinping once called delivery workers “hardworking little bees”; here, the community built them resting stations, including the one near the MixC shopping center, shaped like a beehive. When the district launched its Qianxin program, a rider named Zhu Qiang said: “It gives us a home in the city.” Workers waiting between orders had nowhere to shelter from wind and rain. Shopkeepers, worried that soaked riders might disturb their business, were often reluctant to let them inside. The community decided to build a place along the routes the workers already traveled. “With the station, it is as if we built them a warm harbor right where they must pass,” Secretary Yin said of the station built in the Xingfuli residential block. Inside are air conditioning, drinking water, a microwave, charging facilities, first-aid supplies, and a library stocked with books. Around it, the community has organized an alliance of businesses offering services and discounts. A rider can eat his fill at a participating canteen for fifteen yuan, compared with twenty or thirty for other customers. Some education providers offer half-price courses for workers’ children. Lawyers and family-education counselors hold weekly consultations, while online links connect workers to departments responsible for insurance, schooling, and employment. At the compound entrance, a rider-friendly map marks building entrances and nearby places where riders can rest. A few minutes lost searching for an apartment can mean a late order. “For them, time is money,” Yin explained. The community began by making itself easier for the workers to navigate. Kang Jiafei’s name on the grid board represents another step: the recognition that delivery workers are also contributors to collective life of the city beyond the services they perform for customers. For Yin, this is a reciprocal process. “Everything is two-way,” she explained. By making the community more welcoming to riders, she believes their sense of social responsibility has gradually grown. She described how the relationship developed over three years. Initially, riders found it difficult to join community activities, their working hours too fragmented and unpredictable. Today, when the community announces free medical examinations in their WeChat group, workers invite one another and arrive together. Workers also contact Yin directly about developments around the shopping district. Yin says she has gained not only partners in community work, but also “brothers and sisters.” This is not a charity story. A bench, a socket, a microwave, and a bookshelf are material provisions for workers whose lives are organized around delivering the next order. But they also create spaces where otherwise dispersed workers can meet, develop social relationships, and participate in collective activities. The station becomes more than a place of rest: it becomes an organizational center. The methodology is Party-building adapted to a workforce that the factory no longer houses. The trade unions, Women’s Federation, and Communist Youth League are part of this wider effort to extend organization into new employment groups. Where conditions for establishing Party branches do not yet exist, other mass organizations can provide an institutional foundation. Party members among the delivery workers, like Kang, retain their primary organizational affiliations while participating in activities near their workplaces. The station holds “mini-Party lessons,” between orders – adapting political education to workers whose “time is fragmented and space is fluid,” as Yin put it. The challenge is not only to extend social protections, but also to overcome the atomization produced by platform labor. The algorithms organize riders as individual units of labor, each racing against the clock. The community attempts to bring them into social relationships and institutions that extend beyond the commercial transaction. The contradictions have not disappeared. A subsidized meal does not determine how much a rider earns per delivery, and a rest station cannot replace enforceable labor rights. Those questions remain central to China’s evolving regulation of still-new platform employment. But the community addresses another dimension of the problem: how workers who spend their days moving through a city can become recognized participants in its collective life. The community where Kang Jiafei runs his route is called Xingfuli – “Happiness Lane.” Ninety-two years after the Red Army set off on the historic Long March from this very region, the long work of socialist construction continues in different forms: investigating new conditions, building new institutions, and organizing a changing working class, one neighborhood and one hive at a time. Tings Chak 翟庭君 is the Asia Co-Coordinator of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and an editor of Wenhua Zongheng: A Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought . This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Trump-nominated WFP head has no credible plan to address fund crunch
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: “The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict that is happening all around the world,” Luke Lindberg, the new executive director of the World Food Program (WFP), said in his first media address last week. Conflict is the main driver of hunger today, driving two-thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide. “Conflict is a man-made situation. It is something that we can solve,” added Lindberg, who assumed office on October 26. Earlier this year, the WFP said that the “conflict in the Middle East” – a catch-all phrase for Israeli genocide in Gaza, US-Israeli war on Iran, and the Saudi war on Yemen – “is deepening this food crisis to an alarming degree,” warning of “record numbers of acute hunger if it continues.”​ On the heels of this threat, El Niño will likely push another 49 million into acute food insecurity, warned Lindberg. Identifying Sudan, South Sudan, and Somalia – all in Africa – as the worst cases to prioritize, he said that his first visit as the head of WFP will be to Sudan, where the world’s hunger crisis is unfolding as the civil war fueled and funded by foreign powers continues into its fourth year. “A pat on the back” instead of the much-needed funding The reason for his travel, he explained, will be to give the frontline humanitarian workers “a pat on the back” and say “thank you for your service.” However, humanitarian workers in Sudan need more than a pat on the back. They need funding, which has been reduced by half. Following an eight-day visit to Sudan in September, Lindberg’s predecessor, Carl Skau, the then Acting Executive Director of the WFP, complained that the organization was being forced to cut back on food assistance due to fund cuts. “We now have the capacity, we have the presence, but we are not fully using that space because of the lack of funding.” He warned of the risk that “we will have to scale back even further,” he said . The WFP’s total budget dropped from nearly $9.76 billion in 2024 to $6.52 billion in 2025 to less than $5.89 billion in 2026, as of November 3. Most of this decline is driven by the Trump administration’s fund cuts. The US – whose population of just over 4% of the world owns almost 36% of global personal wealth – has historically been the WFP’s largest donor, funding nearly half of its budget. The Trump administration slashed over half of its funding to the WFP in 2025, reducing it to $2.06 billion from almost $4.5 billion in 2024 . This year, it has contributed just over $1.7 billion .​ Lindberg had served as Trump’s Under Secretary of Agriculture for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs from August 2025 to September 2026, when he resigned to head the WFP. ​ Several reporters asked Lindberg if he would use his close relation to the Trump administration to re-secure the funds the US has slashed.​ MAGA support for humanitarian work? ​ “There is a concept out there that the Republican side is not as interested [in humanitarian work].” But, he claimed, a survey by Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation earlier this year had shown that “79% of self-identified MAGA Republicans support US engagement overseas.”​ However, the survey had not asked about support for humanitarian work. The “ Reagan National Defense Survey ” had found that 79% of MAGA Republicans said that the US “should be more engaged and take the lead in international affairs” As subsequent questions in the survey made clear, this greater engagement and taking the lead in international affairs translated into expanding its military power to be able to fight Russia, China, and use force in Latin America and the Caribbean. After misusing this survey to indicate that Trump’s core voters support US humanitarian funding, Lindberg went on to clarify that he indeed has “great relations with many members of the Trump administration.” “President Trump personally called me and asked me to be the US nominee” for WFP’s executive director, he added. “I know that all the way up the chain to the president there are people within the US government that want to support humanitarian work around the world.”​ No commitment to reverse US fund cuts Nonetheless, he wouldn’t commit to leverage any of this to try to re-secure US funding. Instead, he went on to say, “I look forward to them continuing to play a critical role, but the reality is there are more countries around the world as well … We need to be building that deeper donor partnership.” However, following in the footsteps of the US, other leading donors have also slashed their funding. Germany, which was the second largest donor in 2024, providing $990.9 million in funds to the WFP, reduced it to just over $570 million in 2025. This year, it has provided under $331.4 million. The UK, the third-largest donor in 2024 when it funded over $609.9 million, reduced its donation to $435.16 million in 2025, and to just over USD 220 million so far this year. France in the same period slashed its funding from $196.58 million to USD 113.61 million, to just over $32.5 million. Nevertheless, Lindberg had found “a bright spot.” The WFP, he said, “has done a remarkable job of increasing private sector engagement. The private sector is now the fifth largest donor.” However, private sector funding of the WFP has not shown any meaningful increase since 2024, when it was the fifth largest donor, funding $335.63 million. In 2025, its funding dropped to just over $310 million. It went up in 2026 to $326.07 million, but remains below the 2024 level as of November 3. The rise in the share of WFP budget coming from private sector donations – from 3.44% in 2024 to 4.75% in 2025 to 5.5% in 2026 – has not been driven by an increase in their funding to the WFP. It is rather caused by the decline in the WFP’s total budget from almost $9.6 billion in 2024 to under $5.82 billion this year. Nonetheless, “I think there is a lot more room to grow on that front,” Lindberg said, at a time when WFP’s funding to Sudan has been halved . In South Sudan, over a million people are at risk of losing assistance. Lack of funds is also forcing the WFP to scale down its reach in Somalia to just 5% of the people facing emergency hunger. It has also been forced to reduce its food assistance to Gaza by a third and to the West Bank by half .

articles.title: Schumer & Jeffries reap the backlash to the genocide they enabled
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: Democrats just flipped Congress in a landslide, turned Texas blue, and won a Kansas Senate seat for the first time in nearly a century. But as Rania Khalek explains, the leaders of the new majority on Capitol Hill are the same “corporate suits” who armed Israel through the genocide in Gaza before losing to Trump in 2024, backing record ICE funding through 2029, and sitting on their hands while the administration tore the country and the world apart. Khalek lays out how midterm voters delivered a massive rebuke to Trump’s war on Iran, ICE terror, and soaring cost of living, electing insurgent progressives across the country. But Chuck Schumer insists “the issue is not me,” as Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson and Adam Hamilton say they won’t back him for majority leader. And presumptive House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries thinks when it comes to holding Trump administration officials accountable, Americans “don’t want us to get even.” So what will Democrats actually do with this mandate? Will they investigate and prosecute MAGA crimes, cut off war funding, and break with AIPAC? Or will leadership smother the insurgent wave before it even reaches Washington? “I am absolutely elated – but I’m also cringing because people like Chuck Schumer are reaping the benefits of the backlash to Trump after taking zero accountability for the horrors their party unleashed.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today! #breakthroughnews ****** Rough transcript follows: Democrats won the Senate with 54 seats to 44 seats, and we’re still waiting on Alaska and Mississippi. Democrats are leading in both, so we’ll see how that turns out. They also took the House with 240 seats called so far, and NBC projects they’ll end up around 258 seats, which is a supermajority. Even Texas turned blue, indicating a massive mandate. The question is, what will they do with that mandate? While it’s satisfying to see certain figures defeated, there’s concern about leaders like Chuck Schumer, who still support war and genocide, benefiting from the backlash to Trump without taking accountability for past actions. The corporate Democratic leadership started a genocide in Gaza, lost to fascists, and did little while Trump caused chaos. Now, they’re trying to claim this backlash as a victory, but they’re still quite disliked. This election was also a rejection of them, as many Democratic insurgent candidates won across the country. The point is, this is not the time to relax. It’s time to get organized because leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries may try to obstruct significant changes. The mainstream media is already trying to discipline and tame the more progressive winners of this election. For example, CNN asked James Talarico, now a senator-elect in Texas, if he’ll stand up to the Democrats in Washington. [Speaker 2:] “I will stand up to anyone I have to, to defend the people of Texas. I will work with anyone I can to help the people of Texas. This is what I’ve done for four terms in the state house, long before the Senate race and before doing interviews on CNN.” As for Schumer, when asked about new Democrats who want him out as leader, he said: [Speaker 3:] “The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader. The issue is focusing on the American people and what they want.” Some Democrats are ready for a fight. Robert Garcia, about to chair the House Oversight Committee, has vowed to take on the Trump crime family, corporate corruption, ICE, DHS abuses, and the Epstein coverups. He released a statement with two words: “Lawyer up,” speaking directly to Trump. However, Hakeem Jeffries, expected to become Speaker of the House, said: [Speaker 4:] “The American people don’t want us to get even. They want us to get things done on their behalf because life is way too expensive. We ran on affordability, won on affordability, and now it’s our job to govern on affordability.” This attitude is not surprising from Jeffries, who is a major recipient of corporate PAC money and pro-Israel lobby funds. He has been an ardent supporter of Israeli actions, even during conflicts like Operation Protective Edge in 2014. Let’s listen to a clip of him during a pro-Israel rally: [Speaker 5:] “Israel faced aggression in 1948 and prevailed. In 1967, Israel prevailed. In 1973, Israel prevailed. During the first and second intifadas, Israel prevailed. Missiles flew in 2008 and 2012, and Israel prevailed. I’m confident we’ll stand together: Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever.” This phrasing echoes segregationist George Wallace’s infamous quote. Yet, progressive Democrats like AOC and Brad Lander insist on voting for Jeffries as speaker without conditions. Zoran, who isn’t even in Congress, is pushing for him as well. We’ll see what insurgent Democrats like Claire Valdez and others do. If they let Jeffries become speaker, little will change. A petition circulating online has over 500,000 signatures to appoint someone more progressive than Jeffries as speaker. Chuck Schumer also supports the genocide in Gaza. Here’s what he said about Palestinians: [Speaker 6:] “The view of Palestinians is simple: Europeans treated Jews badly, culminating in the Holocaust, and gave them our land as compensation. We say it’s our land; the Torah says it, but they don’t believe in the Torah. That’s why there’s no peace. We must stand strong with Israel through thick and thin.” This statement is problematic. Schumer calls himself the guardian of Israel and has built his career around protecting it in Congress. He should not be the Democratic leader in the Senate. Some Senate Democrats, like Adam Hamilton and others, oppose him, but he claims he has the majority support needed. Corporate figures like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer represent what the Democratic Party stands for now. In Israel, there’s panic, but not everyone is worried. Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid tweeted: [Speaker 7:] “Hakeem Jeffries will lead the House. Chuck Schumer will run the Senate. Both are my friends and voted with Israel this year. They’re leaders Israel should work with, even if we don’t agree on everything. The anti-Israel core in the House has grown, but it’s a small minority.” Only 13% of Democrats have a positive view of Israel, yet this minority runs the party. AIPAC bragged that more than 234 candidates supported by its members have won. This party won’t voluntarily give people what they want. They govern for the ruling class, not for us. Their leadership opposes universal healthcare, capping prescription drug prices, taxing billionaires, cutting off Israel, and ending wars. We need to build outside this decrepit Republican-lite party, or we’ll stay stuck in a cycle of liberal to fascist until it’s just fascist.
